items.title: Why I Love Imperfect Photos
items.summary: Take a look at the three unedited photos below. Technically speaking, none of them are "perfect." They aren't sharp—at least not in that hyper-crisp, digital way we’re used to seeing all over social media and in magazines these days. There's a reason for that. I…
items.content_html:
Take a look at the three unedited photos below.
 
 
 
 
 
Technically speaking, none of them are "perfect." They aren't sharp—at least not in that hyper-crisp, digital way we’re used to seeing all over social media and in magazines these days. There's a reason for that. I shot these photos on old film cameras using ISO 100 film. This forced me to use slower shutter speeds, and less depth of field. On top of that, vintage lenses simply don't have that clinical, razor-sharp edge that modern lenses do.
 
But you know what? I absolutely love these little imperfections.
To me, the lack of clinical sharpness is exactly what gives these images their soul, energy, and character. There is an organic warmth to them, and I just know they would look incredible printed the traditional way in a darkroom.
 
The great Henri Cartier-Bresson once called sharpness a "bourgeois concept," and I couldn't agree more. I'm not just echoing his words, either—I’ve lived by this exact same philosophy for over twenty years, long before I ever came across his famous quote.
Don't get me wrong, there is a time and a place for technical perfection. When doing a commercial commission, shooting products, or capturing interiors, the images need to be pin-sharp. Period. I completely get that. But at its heart, photography isn't about chasing sharpness, tweaking color profiles, or slapping on digital filters to manufacture a certain "look." It’s not about the gear, and it's definitely not about the technical specs of the camera. To me, photography is a language to share an emotion, a mood, and above all, a feeling. And honestly, I usually find a lot more feeling in imperfection. After all, what’s the point of a technically flawless photo if it doesn't make you feel anything?
As Daido Moriyama once beautifully pointed out, you can write the most breathtaking poem with the cheapest ballpoint pen. His argument: It’s never about the tools you hold - it’s about the story you want to tell.
 
I believe there's beauty in simplicity, especially when it comes to photography - and I'll go a step further and say it applies to all art forms. There's a profound power in understatement; in leaving something unsaid so that the message resonates louder and clearer. That is exactly what these technically unsharp photos do for me, and it's why they possess such incredible staying power. And I'm not alone in this. It is the exact reason why we still stare in awe at a man leaping over a puddle in Paris, or American soldiers struggling through the crashing waves of Omaha Beach. Those iconic pictures aren't sharp, and because they aren't, they force the mind and the heart to sharpen instead - compelling us to truly feel the story.
 
That is why a raw, imperfect photograph will always triumph over the clinical world of over-edited, hyper-focused, digital-color-profile-infested camera recipes. You can engineer perfection, but you cannot manufacture feeling.

Long live imperfection.

items.title: Sun, Shadows and Stone: An afternoon at Valle dei Templi
items.summary: As we drive into the parking lot of the Valle dei Templi, there's sand and dust everywhere. It's early August and Ferragosto hasn't started yet, but it feels like the whole of Italy has planned to come here today. Cars crisscross the terrain like ants,…
items.content_html:
As we drive into the parking lot of the Valle dei Templi, there's sand and dust everywhere. It's early August and Ferragosto hasn't started yet, but it feels like the whole of Italy has planned to come here today. Cars crisscross the terrain like ants, and — in typical Sicilian fashion — there's little signage to tell you where to go. After all these years of traveling to Sicily, I've grown used to a bit of organized chaos. I like it, actually. It makes the island feel so much like itself — a stark contrast to the planned, orderly street architecture I'm used to in the Netherlands.

Today I won't have many opportunities to take photos. Still, when the moment arises, I attempt a few shots. I don't want to disturb our guide as he talks — which he does so well — walking us through the complete history of the valley in just over two hours. For the pictures I do manage to shoot, I've set my camera to RAW. It helps preserve the highlights under this burning sun. What I sometimes like to do in these situations is shoot deliberately into the sun. It gives you a silhouetted foreground, and paired with a vintage 50mm Takumar lens, it creates a really beautiful, warm vintage look.

We conclude the day entirely satisfied. This was such a rich experience. It's incredible to witness how these ancient structures have survived destruction, wars, and natural disasters over the millennia, yet they are still standing — a testament to the people who built them. They knew a thing or two about construction, and so much more besides: agriculture, astronomy, mathematics — things we, 2000 years later, can still learn from. This visit definitely deserves a follow-up in the form of a good book about these temples. Or who knows — perhaps I'll visit them again someday. They're not in a hurry, after all.

For now, it's back to the dusty parking lot to queue up with my ant friends. I forget about the ancient Greeks for a moment as my mind slowly drifts to granitas and an ice-cold Peroni.
